# Qualifying event scenarios

General rules for employers and HR, reviewed against the citations below in October 2026. The employer's plan document and the carrier's rules govern. This is not legal or tax advice.

Path count: 6966.

## Result counts

- allowed: 648
- carrier: 194
- eligibility: 152
- late: 616
- need_fact: 1253
- not_permitted: 2502
- plan: 308
- split: 1293

## What changed and why

- The page is full width, with the same navy banner, gold rule, eyebrow, serif title, white cards, and stepper as the other DK Benefits tools. The old tool was a fixed 639 by 720 box with an inner scrollbar and a blank gap under the choices.
- The step counter lists the same steps as the stepper, including the result. The old screen said Step 1 of 4 next to five dots.
- Emoji choices are gone. Choices are text, in the same pattern as the Section 128 and wrap plan tools.
- Gold actions use #16233A text and do not use a blue focus outline.
- The page posts its height so the Wix shim can size the frame. The tool itself does not scroll inside a short panel.
- Over 30 days now reads as past the standard window, generally not allowed unless the plan allows a longer window. It does not say the request is illegal.
- Medicaid and CHIP loss of eligibility, and premium assistance, use 60 days. Coverage is effective no later than the first of the month after the plan receives the request. Medicare is its own event and uses the normal window. Gaining Medicaid is a reason to drop or reduce that person, not a 60-day enrollment right.
- A drop after someone gains other coverage is allowed only for the people that other plan covers.
- Marriage can add the spouse's children, enroll an employee who had waived, and switch benefit package. Coverage starts no later than the first of the next month after the request, not on the wedding date.
- Birth, adoption, and placement can enroll the employee and spouse as well as the child, and the elected coverage starts on the event date. A drop is not allowed for the birth itself.
- Divorce lets the employee remove the former spouse. The removal is effective under the plan's eligibility rule, and the Section 125 election uses the standard 30-day window. A late report gets that window answer, plus one line telling HR to ask the carrier whether it will accept a late or retro removal and what its policy is. The carrier question is not the main answer. Divorce still does not let the employee drop themselves or a child who is still eligible.
- Loss of other coverage now asks why it ended. Eligibility losses, the other employer stopping contributions, and exhaustion of COBRA can be special enrollment. A chosen drop, nonpayment, or fraud is not. Ending COBRA early is not exhaustion.
- Job and hours changes now separate a new eligibility, a lost eligibility, an hour cut where the employee stays eligible (Notice 2014-55 only if the plan was amended), FMLA, and USERRA.
- Death asks who died. Removing someone still living is not allowed. Death of the employee points to COBRA for survivors.
- A court order can enroll a child, and can remove a child only when the order requires someone else to cover the child and that coverage is in place.
- Cost changes are changes the employer makes during the year, such as raising premiums or cutting its contribution, under Treas. Reg. 1.125-4(f). An employee who changes their own tier or class is handled as a change in employment status, not as a cost change. Coverage changes follow the curtailment, new-option, and other-employer rules. A health FSA cannot be changed for those events.
- Dependent care has its own answers, including a non-relative rate change, a provider change, and a child turning 13.
- An HSA paycheck change is prospective and does not need a qualifying event. After-tax benefits outside the cafeteria plan follow the carrier, not a blanket "generally allowed." Pre-tax voluntary benefits still follow Section 125.
- The result screen keeps the link to the Section 125 plan document tool. No contact form was added. `window.QE.scenario` holds the event, change, timing, coverage, follow-ups, and result for a later form.

## Points that need a human confirmation

- Whether a particular dental or vision plan is an excepted benefit. That decides whether HIPAA special enrollment forces the carrier to enroll.
- What a plan treats as a significant cost increase. The regulation does not set a percentage. The tool treats the event as the employer changing the cost, and sends an employee tier or class change to the job event.
- A health FSA decrease when medical coverage moves to a spouse's plan. An increase on marriage is in the examples. That decrease is less explicit, so the tool says to check the document.
- Notice 2014-55 is optional, needs an amendment, and depends on the employee's other coverage starting on time. The tool does not decide affordability or full-time status under section 4980H.
- Proposed cafeteria plan rules are widely followed for monthly HSA election changes. The solid cite used here is IRS Notice 2004-50, Q&A-58, which says the change must be prospective.

## How to read a row

Each row is one path the tool can take. Coverage lists the benefits in that path. The result code is the headline. Bases are the rules the answer uses. The same path is asserted in `qualifying-event/test/paths.test.js`.

Codes: allowed (generally process), late (past the usual window), plan (only if the document, and sometimes a Notice 2014-55 amendment, allows it), eligibility (process because the person is no longer eligible or an order requires enrollment), not_permitted, need_fact, carrier (after-tax, outside Section 125), split (benefits disagree).
